title: the Yoga Vasistha (selections)
hook: a king bows to a young teacher, never guessing it's his wife
tomorrow: the king is free, alone in a hut. what does a free person do next?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yoga Vasistha's Queen Chudala found freedom at home, and her husband laughed and left for the forest. Today, she follows him.

Decluttering videos make a promise: a bare room means a free mind. Give away the stuff, and the weight goes with it. King Shikhidhvaja tried a version of that. He left a kingdom for a forest hut. Then a young Brahmin walks in, who calls himself Kumbha. The king bows to him as a teacher, never guessing it's Chudala, his own wife, in disguise. She's come to teach the husband who wouldn't hear her at home. Her first question: have you really given up everything?
screen: `A BARE ROOM, A FREE MIND?` → `A YOUNG TEACHER CALLED KUMBHA.` → `HAVE YOU GIVEN UP EVERYTHING?`

segments.voice: Two views of giving up meet in that hut. The king's view: renunciation means leaving things behind. He has paid for it: kingdom, wealth, palace, wife. It isn't foolish. Leaving things behind is real work, and he did it with his whole heart. Kumbha's view: something is still left. So the king looks at what remains, his hut, his staff, his bowl, and he burns them and watches them go. Now? Still not everything, Kumbha says. What's left was never a thing. It's the one doing the holding: the mind that clings, the sense of mine and I. Give that up, Kumbha says, and you've given up everything. The Sanskrit word is tyaga, renunciation. And Kumbha doesn't call the king's way wrong. She says it isn't finished. One view moves outward, one thing at a time, and something is always left. The other turns inward, to the grip itself. Vasistha tells this to Rama, a prince who wanted to walk away from the world, about a king who walked away and was still holding on.
screen: `THE KING: LEAVE THINGS BEHIND.` · `THE HUT, THE STAFF, THE BOWL, BURNED.` · `KUMBHA: THE GRIP IS STILL THERE.` · then, large: `GIVE UP THE GRIP, NOT JUST THE THINGS.`

segments.voice: Pick up something small you'd hate to lose: a ring, your keys, your phone. Hold it tightly in your fist for a few breaths and feel the grip. Then open your hand slowly, so it rests on your open palm, still yours and still there, with only the clutching gone.
The Yoga Vasistha: here, Kumbha's tyaga, giving up not the things but the grip on them.
Your line: the Yoga Vasistha, in selections. Burn the hut, and the grip can still be there. Sixteen-oh-six, done.

screen: `DAY 1606 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DOES A FREE PERSON DO NEXT?`

howItsDone: Hindu tradition honors both kinds of giving up: some take sannyasa and leave home, while householders are taught to act without clinging; teachers often tell Chudala's story to show the second.

notes: Yoga Vasistha run, day 6: Chudala, part two.

Confirm in the Nirvana Prakarana: Chudala travels to the forest and takes the form of a young Brahmin named Kumbha; the king honors him as a teacher; the sequence (kingdom given up; hut and possessions burned); renunciation of all as the giving up of the mind's clinging. Kumbha's stated parentage left out.

Safety (left out on purpose): in the text the king next resolves to cast off his own body, and Kumbha stops him. That self-harm beat is cut from this teen-facing lesson; the teaching (the grip, not the things) stands without it. A Keeper may judge whether the omission changes the story's point.

howItsDone (sannyasa and householders; 'teachers often tell') is general; soften under the claims rule if needed.
